title: On-call & Incident Response Playbook: Ops, Runbooks, Comms and Game Days
author: Maya Thompson
content:
Summary

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's on-call and incident response standards: incident classifications and routing, runbooks for common failures, postmortem template and expectations, on-call rotation rules, game day guidance, and customer/status-page communication templates. It is intended for engineers, SREs, support, and product owners who participate in incident response.

Scope

- Applies to all production-facing Redwood services: API Gateway, Inference Runtime, Model Serving, Fleet Autoscaler, and Console.
- Covers detection -> triage -> mitigation -> recovery -> postmortem and customer communications.
- Excludes internal non-production test environments (see separate dev-runs).

1) Incident severity definitions and routing

- P0 (Sev0): Production outage affecting majority of users or any incident with critical data loss or security impact. Targets: page immediately to primary on-call, notify execs, open high-priority incident bridge.
  - Impact: >50% request failure or total service unavailable.
  - SLA: immediate escalation; restore service within 1 hour target (SLO dependent).

- P1 (Sev1): Major degradation impacting a subset of users or high latency causing significant revenue/experience impact.
  - Impact: 10-50% errors, sustained latency >500ms for critical paths.
  - SLA: page primary on-call; aim for mitigation within 4 hours.

- P2 (Sev2): Functional regression with limited scope; non-critical features degraded.
  - Impact: single-model regressions, background worker failures, or non-urgent alerts.
  - SLA: page on-call if needed; target resolution within 24-72 hours depending on impact.

Routing and ownership

- Primary on-call: first responder for P0/P1.
- Secondary (escalation): engages if primary unavailable after 10 minutes or incident escalated.
- Platform SRE lead: coordinates cross-service mitigation and capacity changes.
- Product/Owner: responsible for user-impact assessment and communications.

2) On-call rotations and responsibilities

Rotation model

- Team-level rotations (two-week cadence recommended).
- Roles per rotation: Primary on-call, Secondary on-call, and Weekend backup (optional).
- Handoff checklist (to be completed in Slack #oncall-handoffs channel):
  1. Confirm runbook access and PagerDuty schedule.
  2. Review active incidents and ongoing mitigations.
  3. Note planned maintenance windows.

Responsibilities

- Primary: respond to pages, triage, run mitigation runbooks, update incident timeline.
- Secondary: available for escalation and deep dives; takes on-call if primary is unavailable.
- Owner/Product: provide impact, prioritize customer comms, and approve postmortem content.

Escalation policy

1. Primary handles initial triage within 10 minutes.
2. If unresolved or critical, escalate to Secondary after 10 minutes or to SRE lead immediately for P0s.
3. Exec notification: triggered for P0s or P1s with >4 hour impact.

3) Incident response process (step-by-step)

Below is the canonical workflow; teams may augment with service-specific steps.

Detection and alerting

- Alerts are routed via PagerDuty and mirrored to #incidents Slack channel.
- Alert thresholds and SLO burn alerts posted to #slo-alerts.

Triage (first 10 minutes)

1. Confirm alert legitimacy: check monitoring dashboards (Grafana), logs (ELK), and traces (Tempo).
2. Assign severity and open incident in Incident Manager (confluence incident ID or Jira incident).
3. Contact Secondary if needed.

Mitigation (minutes to hours)

- Follow an established runbook for the symptom class. If no runbook exists, perform safe mitigation: scale down problematic traffic, activate fallback model variant, enable read-only mode for Console, or route traffic to secondary region.
- Maintain an incident timeline in the incident doc (link in Incident Manager).

Recovery and verification

- Verify service health: end-to-end tests, latency checks, and reduced error rates.
- Gradually roll traffic back to normal and confirm stability for 30 minutes before declaring resolved for P1/P2. For P0 require 60 minutes of stability.

Post-incident activities

- Create a postmortem for all P0/P1 incidents within 72 hours (draft) and publish within 7 days.
- Track action items in the Postmortem and assign ownership with due dates.
- Perform follow-up validation and close action items in three weeks or re-evaluate.

4) Runbooks (common scenarios)

Runbook: API Gateway 5xx spike

- Symptoms:
  - 5xx error rate >5% over 5m for api-gateway-prod
  - Sudden increase in request volume or backend timeouts

- Quick checks:
  1. Grafana: check api-gateway request rate & 5xx graph.
  2. Logs: `kubectl logs -n prod deploy/api-gateway --since=10m | grep ERROR`
  3. Upstream: check inference-runtime latency and model-serving error graphs.

- Mitigation steps:
  1. If upstream timeouts: scale inference-runtime pool (see Autoscale runbook).
  2. If gateway overload: set temporary rate-limit in Envoy config and reload:

```bash
# apply temp rate limit patch
kubectl apply -f /tmp/envoy-rate-limit-patch.yaml -n prod
# restart api-gateway pods gracefully
kubectl rollout restart deployment/api-gateway -n prod
```

- Post-incident:
  - Capture traffic spike source and patch client behavior if needed.
  - Consider adding a circuit-breaker in front of slow upstreams.

Runbook: Inference runtime OOMs on GPU nodes

- Symptoms:
  - GPU OOM OOMKilled events in node logs
  - Drop in concurrent requests handled per instance

- Quick checks:
  1. `kubectl describe pod <pod>` and review OOM logs.
  2. Check model size/quantization profile in model registry.

- Mitigation steps:
  1. Evict offending pods: `kubectl delete pod <pod>` to allow autoscaler to bring up replacements.
  2. If repeated, reduce concurrency or pin to a smaller model variant.
  3. If cluster-wide, add capacity (scale nodepool) or enable temporary batch size reduction in runtime config.

- Post-incident:
  - Update quantization profile or model packaging. Add guardrails to prevent oversized model deployments.

(Each team should maintain a directory of runbooks referenced from the incident index.)

5) Postmortem template and expectations

Create a document in Incident Manager with these headings and fill in all sections for P0/P1: 

- Title (service - short description)
- Incident ID
- Severity
- Summary (one-paragraph impact summary)
- Timeline (UTC timestamps, actions, participants)
- Impact (customers, requests affected, revenue, SLO burn)
- Root cause analysis (technical cause + why safeguards failed)
- Corrective & preventive actions (owner + due date)
- Rollout / verification plan for fixes
- Lessons learned
- Distribution list (who should be notified)

Expectations

- Draft within 72 hours, review with the team within 5 business days, and publish within 7 days.
- Action items tracked to completion; unresolved items reviewed at weekly reliability meeting.

6) Game days and exercises

Objectives

- Validate runbooks, alerting, and cross-team coordination.
- Exercise regional failover, model rollback, and capacity shortage scenarios.

Suggested cadence

- At least one partial-team game day per quarter and one company-wide major exercise annually.
- Use realistic traffic replay where possible.

Sample scenarios

- Model-serving regression: a new model release causes incorrect shard mapping.
- Region outage: simulate single-region AZ failure and fail traffic to secondary region.
- Load surge: sudden 5x traffic spike to inference runtime.

Post-game-day checklist

1. Document findings and gaps.
2. Create action items and assign owners.
3. Update runbooks and alerts based on outcomes.

7) Status page and customer communications templates

Status page fields

- Title, Impacted Services, Start Time, Current Status (Investigating / Identified / Monitoring / Resolved), Root Cause (when available), ETA for resolution, Mitigation steps taken, Next update ETA.

Initial customer message (short, for status page & support ticket)

"We are currently investigating elevated errors and increased latencies for the Redwood API. Some requests may fail or see degraded performance. Our engineering team has been paged and is actively investigating. We'll provide an update within 30 minutes with next steps."

Customer update (progress)

"Update: We have identified a service degradation affecting model inference in region us-west-2. Engineers are applying an emergency mitigation (traffic reroute and model rollback). We expect partial restoration within ~60 minutes. We will provide another update in 30 minutes or sooner if there is a material change."

Resolution message

"Resolved: The issue affecting inference in us-west-2 has been resolved at 2026-02-28T17:12:00Z. The root cause was a misconfiguration in the autoscaler that caused unsafe instance churn. We have deployed a fix and validated traffic return to normal levels. A postmortem will be published within 7 days."

Internal comms (Slack templates)

- P0 notification: `@here P0: <service> outage in <region> — incident open: <link>. Primary: @primary, Secondary: @secondary, SRE Lead: @sre-lead`
- Update template: `INCUPDATE [<HH:MM UTC>] <short summary> | Impact: <# users> | Next: <ETA>`

Status cadence

- P0: updates every 15 minutes until resolved or stable.
- P1: updates every 30-60 minutes.
- P2: as-needed with daily summary for multi-day incidents.

8) Ownership, tooling, and observability

- Tools used: PagerDuty, Jira/Incident Manager, Grafana (SLO & metrics), ELK (logs), Tempo (traces), Statuspage (customer-facing).
- Incident index: maintain list of active and historical incidents with links to runbooks and postmortems.
- Runbook storage: central repo under confluence /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks (team-level mirrors recommended).

9) Appendix: Useful commands and quick references

- Check API gateway errors: `kubectl -n prod get pods | grep api-gateway`
- Restart a deployment: `kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name> -n prod`
- Scale nodepool (GKE example): `gcloud container clusters resize <cluster> --node-pool <pool> --num-nodes <n> --zone <zone>`

Etiquette and psychological safety

- Prioritize safety: no blaming in public docs or channels. Focus on fixes and learning.
- During incidents, designate a communications owner so engineers can focus on mitigation.

Document maintenance

- Owners: team on-call leads are responsible for keeping runbooks current.
- Review cadence: runbooks reviewed quarterly; on-call playbook reviewed semi-annually.

Related resources

- Link to SLOs and error budgets: /confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets
- Runbook directory: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks
- Incident Manager template: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-manager-template
